cards.back: Interval of 7 semitones, e.g. C to G.
Interval of 4 semitones, e.g. C to E.
Interval of 3 semitones, e.g. A to C.
Interval of 6 semitones: an augmented fourth or diminished fifth.
The interval numbers add up to 9; major becomes minor, augmented becomes diminished, perfect stays perfect.
An interval larger than an octave, e.g. a major ninth.
Interval of 5 semitones, e.g. C to F.
Interval of 10 semitones, e.g. G to F.
Consonant: unisons, thirds, sixths, perfect fifths, octaves. Dissonant: seconds, sevenths, the tritone.
Root, major third and perfect fifth (C–E–G).
Root, minor third and perfect fifth (A–C–E).
Root, minor third and diminished fifth (B–D–F).
Root, major third and augmented fifth (C–E–G#).
A major triad plus a minor seventh, built on the fifth degree (G–B–D–F in C major).
The third of the chord is in the bass; figured bass 6.
The fifth of the chord is in the bass; figured bass 6/4.
Numbers under a bass line showing the intervals above it, which tell you the chord.
A major chord on the flattened second degree, in first inversion.
A stack of minor thirds, built on the leading note in the harmonic minor.
Tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone, tone, semitone.
The natural minor with a raised seventh degree, giving an augmented second between 6 and 7.
Raised sixth and seventh going up; natural minor coming down.
The minor key that shares the key signature of a major key, a minor third below (A minor for C major).
F C G D A E B
B E A D G C F
Keys arranged by perfect fifths; each step clockwise adds a sharp to the key signature.
Two sharps: F# and C#.
The seventh degree of the scale, a semitone below the tonic.
All twelve semitones in an octave.
A five-note scale; the major pentatonic uses degrees 1 2 3 5 6.
Tonic, supertonic, mediant, subdominant, dominant, submediant, leading note.
The natural minor with a raised sixth; D to D on the white notes.
The major scale with a flattened seventh; G to G on the white notes.
The major scale with a raised fourth; F to F on the white notes.
The natural minor with a flattened second; E to E on the white notes.
The natural minor scale; A to A on the white notes.
B to B on the white notes; a diminished fifth above the tonic.
V–I: dominant chord to tonic chord; sounds finished.
IV–I: the "Amen" cadence.
Ends on V; sounds unfinished, like a comma.
V–VI: the music seems about to end but goes to the submediant chord.
IVb–V in a minor key: a kind of imperfect cadence.
Ending a minor-key piece on a major tonic chord.
Ic–V–I: a second inversion tonic chord before the dominant at a cadence.
Simple: the beat divides into two (2/4, 3/4, 4/4). Compound: the beat divides into three (6/8, 9/8, 12/8).
Compound duple time: two dotted crotchet beats in a bar.
Simple triple time: three crotchet beats in a bar.
Accenting off-beats or weak beats.
Two bars of triple time felt as three bars of duple time.
An upbeat: the note or notes before the first strong beat of a bar.
A dot adds half the note's value: a dotted minim lasts 3 crotchets.
Three notes played in the time of two of the same value.
e.g. 5/4 or 7/8: the beats are grouped unevenly.
Two voices moving in perfect fifths; avoided in four-part harmony.
A note held over from the previous chord to make a dissonance, which then resolves down by step.
A non-chord note moving by step between two chord notes.
An accented non-chord note approached by leap and resolved by step.
Usually double the root; avoid doubling the leading note.
A sustained or repeated bass note while the harmony changes above it.
Fast, lively.
At a walking pace.
Gradually getting louder.
Gradually getting slower.
Smoothly.
Short and detached.
